labels.name: bug

labels.name: server
labels.description: iggy-server related change

items.body:
### Bug description

`handle_prepare_timeout` (`core/consensus/src/impls.rs:2918-2967`) retransmits to every replica missing an ack, including the primary itself, and a send to self is a no-op (`core/shard/src/lib.rs:11635`). When all remote acks are in and the primary's own journal write is the laggard, the timer only backs off and the op does not commit.

The metadata plane papers over the durable case with `repair_primary_self_acks` (`core/metadata/src/impls/metadata.rs:3053`), which re-acks ops the primary already holds durably but does not retry a lagging write. The partition plane has no equivalent and fences the partition fatal instead (`core/partitions/src/iggy_partition.rs:5411-5425`).

### Affected area / component

Iggy server (consensus, both planes)

### Proposed solution

In `handle_prepare_timeout`, when the only missing ack is the primary's own, emit a `RetryLocalWrite { op }` action instead of `RetransmitPrepares`, and let the shard re-append and self-ack. Drop self from the retransmit targets.

### Alternatives considered

Port `repair_primary_self_acks` to the partition plane, which covers the durable-but-unacked case only. Keep the fatal fence.

### Description

Both torn-tail specs in `core/integration/tests/cluster/crash_recovery_corruption.rs` tear a backup's segment and restart that backup. Nothing tears the leader's active segment. A leader that recovers from a torn tail has to serve reads and drive repair from the reopened segment, which is a different path from a backup catching up, and no test covers it.

### Proposed solution

Add a primary-side variant of at least the `.log` case: tear the leader's active segment, restart that node, and assert the same contract the backup specs assert (survives the next restart, every acked offset still reads back, at-rest bytes match across replicas).

### Affected area / component

Integration tests, Iggy server (segment recovery)

## Which issue does this PR address?

Relates to #4438

## Rationale

CONTRIBUTING asks that a bug found with an agent comes with failing tests first, and the fix after the direction is agreed on the issue. This PR adds only the tests. It does not include a fix.

## What changed?

After rolling crash-restarts under load, a restarted partition replica can need state transfer and never finish it, while it keeps serving its stale prefix (#4438). Three separate livelocks cause this. This PR adds one deterministic test per livelock. Each test is marked `#[ignore = "#4438: ..."]`, so default CI stays green and `--ignored` runs them. Each test has a `TODO(#4438)` with the suggested fix direction.

- `iggy_partition::tests::given_commit_max_advanced_during_the_pull_when_installing_should_land_and_leave_the_tail_to_repair`: `install_state_transfer` refuses an offer below the receiver's `commit_max` even when its sequencer is below the offer, so the install would erase nothing. Fails today with `StaleTransfer { commit_op: 1, commit_min: 4 }`.
- `poll::completion_tests::given_the_primary_offer_when_this_replica_ratcheted_its_view_alone_should_accept_it` (shard crate): drives `on_partition_state_transfer_target` with the group primary's descriptor (view 20, higher `commit_max`) at a replica whose log view is 11 but whose own view reached 58 through elections nobody heard. The gate compares against `view()` and refuses the offer, so the session is never accepted.
- `iggy_partition::tests::given_a_resident_leading_edge_above_durable_end_when_the_window_is_longer_than_a_chunk_should_refuse_commit_floor`: the first repair chunk is resident and its first batch starts above the recovered durable end, but the window spans more than one chunk. `complete_repair` returns `InProgress` instead of `FloorRefused`. The next chunk is requested only when the commit walk advances, which the refused floor prevents, so the replica never escalates to state transfer.

The partition-descriptor test sits next to the existing metadata-descriptor test in `poll/completion_tests.rs`, because that module already has the owner-shard harness for calling a descriptor handler.

items.title: Partition replica stuck after rolling crash-restarts: state transfer never completes while it keeps serving its stale prefix
items.body:
### Bug description

After rolling crash-restarts under produce load, a restarted partition replica can stay behind its group for good. It keeps serving the partition, so readers that poll it stop at its stale prefix while the other two replicas hold the full log.

On restart, the replica's durable state ends below the repair window that its peers still retain. It refuses the commit floor and asks for a state transfer:

```
refusing commit floor: repaired window does not connect to recovered durable state (needs state transfer)
```

The state transfer never completes, and the replica does not escalate or step aside. It keeps answering polls up to its own `commit_min`.

No acknowledged data is lost with `persisted` durability: restarting only the lagging node made every acknowledged event readable again. Before that restart, about half of the acknowledged events could not be read through the stuck replica.

**Expected:** the restarted replica installs a state transfer (or repairs) and catches up with its group.
**Actual:** it stays at its stale prefix until an operator restarts it.

### Affected area / component

Clustering / replication (partition plane: journal repair and state transfer)

### Deployment

Compiled from source, 3 `iggy-server` processes in Docker containers on one host.

### Versions

`master` @ `f6dfbdbb3`. The code paths described below are unchanged on current `master` (`43fb44364`); see the failing tests in #4439.

### Hardware / environment

Linux x86_64, local disk. Each node is a container limited to 2 CPU and 4 GiB of memory.

### Reproduction

1. Start a 3-node cluster.
2. Create one stream and one topic with 1 partition and `--durability persisted`.
3. Produce at a combined 30,000 msg/s for 360 s: 12 producers, batches of 100.
4. During the load, SIGKILL the nodes one at a time, 80 s apart. Keep each node down for 40 s, then restart it from its data directory. That is: kill node 0 at 80 s, start it at 120 s, kill node 1 at 200 s, start it at 240 s, kill node 2 at 320 s, start it at 360 s.
5. After the load stops, read the partition from offset 0 and compare against every acknowledged message.

Results:

- Plain `f6dfbdbb3`: 1 of 2 runs failed. 2,283,600 of 4,570,200 acknowledged events were unreadable. Two nodes held an identical 1.62 GB on disk, the lagging node 0.80 GB. After a restart of only the lagging node, 0 of 4,570,200 events were missing.
- A build with additional, unrelated changes: 4 of 4 runs failed with the same signature.

The failure is timing dependent. It needs a restarted replica whose recovered segments end below the oldest op that its peers still retain in their repair ring, which is likely at this write rate.

### Logs

On the lagging node, repeated for minutes (messages verbatim, structured fields abbreviated):

```
refusing commit floor: repaired window does not connect to recovered durable state (needs state transfer)
partition state transfer install failed; falling back to journal repair  error="transfer frontier 34274 is below the local commit frontier 36787"
refusing a partition transfer offer from a replica behind this one  serving_view=20 local_view=58
```

In one run the third line appeared 117 times, while the serving primary at view 20 already had a higher `commit_max` than the lagging replica. In another run, after the first two causes below were removed, the first line repeated 239 times over 3.5 minutes with no state transfer request at all.

### Analysis

This section is my analysis. I found three separate livelocks in the state-transfer path. Each one alone keeps the replica behind. #4439 adds one failing test per livelock, marked `#[ignore = "#<this issue>: ..."]`.

1. **The install refuses an offer once `commit_max` moves past it during the pull** (`core/partitions/src/state_transfer.rs`, `install_state_transfer`). The serving primary builds the offer at its `commit_min`. The pull takes 10 to 20 s under load, because the active segment alone is hundreds of MiB. Meanwhile, the primary's commit heartbeats raise the receiver's `commit_max`. The install refuses any `commit_op < commit_max`, so every round fails with `transfer frontier X is below the local commit frontier Y`, and the next round is just as far behind.
   The guard exists so that the rewind to `commit_op` never erases an op that this replica may have acked and knows is committed. A backup acks only ops at or below its sequencer, so those ops are in `(commit_op, min(commit_max, sequencer)]`. A gap-stopped receiver has its sequencer below the offer, so the install erases nothing. The committed tail above the offer is what journal repair fetches after the install, as the install's doc comment already describes.
   Suggested direction: refuse only when `commit_op < min(commit_max, sequencer)`. A primary's sequencer is at least its `commit_max`, so primaries keep the current behavior.

2. **The descriptor gate compares the offer with a view that the replica raised alone** (`core/shard/src/lib.rs`, `on_partition_state_transfer_target`). A replica that needs state transfer cannot finish a view change. With `persisted` durability it cannot vote in one either: its WAL cannot certify a holed log, so every view-scoped send is withheld. Its elections time out with nobody hearing them, and its `view` keeps rising (58 against the primary's 20 in the run above). The gate refuses an offer with `serving_view < local view`, so it refuses every offer from the group's real primary, even when that offer holds more committed state.
   Suggested direction: compare the serving view with the local `log_view` (the last view whose log this replica adopted). That still refuses a phantom view-0 primary, an offer from before the adopted view, and any offer below the local `commit_max`.
   Related: the same ratcheted `view()` picks the "known primary" when a transfer is re-armed (the transient-refusal branch of `on_partition_state_transfer_target`, and `next_transfer_peer` in the re-arm path). So the replica can also rotate away from the real primary.

3. **A refused commit floor never becomes definitive when the repair window is longer than one chunk** (`core/partitions/src/iggy_partition.rs`, `complete_repair`). A floor refusal converts to a state transfer only when the whole window `(floor, to_op]` is resident, because a later frame could still lower `first_batch_offset` into connection. But the next 128-op repair chunk is requested only when the commit walk advances, and a refused floor never lets it advance. So every stall retry fetches the same first chunk, and the window never completes. Under load the serving peer eventually evicts the whole window, which empties it and ends the wait. After load stops, the replica refuses the floor forever and never asks for a transfer.
   Suggested direction: record the op whose batch set `first_batch_offset`. Offsets rise with ops, so once every op in `(floor, that op)` is resident, no later frame can lower the first batch offset, and the refusal is final.

None of these changes serves or acknowledges anything new. Directions 1 and 2 decide which committed state a receiver may install. Direction 3 decides when to start a transfer.

With all three changes applied on top of `f6dfbdbb3` plus unrelated changes, the same scenario passed 3 of 3 runs with 0 lost events, and all three replicas ended with identical segment bytes. In each run the lagging replica needed a state transfer 2 to 26 times and installed it within 10 to 20 s while the load continued.

A separate question: should a replica that knows it needs state transfer keep serving reads for the partition? Its data is committed, so it is stale but never wrong. But a consumer that polls only that replica sees the partition stop.

### Contribution

- [x] I'm willing to submit a pull request to fix this bug

I have the fix for all three, with tests, and can open it once the direction is agreed here.

items.title: Rust SDK: sends to a multi-partition topic bounce between nodes once partition primaries diverge (multi-second stalls)
items.body:
## Bug description

In a cluster, a Rust SDK producer that writes to several partitions of one topic
stalls for about 4 seconds on nearly every send once those partitions' primaries
are on different nodes. Each send moves the client's only connection to another
node.

Each partition is its own consensus group and elects its own primary. On a fresh
cluster all partition primaries are on one node, so every send is admitted where
the client is connected. After failovers (for example, nodes restarted one at a
time) the primaries end up on different nodes. Polls handle this: `PollRouter`
(`core/sdk/src/poll_routing.rs`) sends a poll to the partition's primary over a
separate data connection and keeps the session where it is. Sends have no
equivalent. `SendMessages` goes out on the one TCP session:

1. The client is on node A. It sends to partition 0, whose primary is node B.
   Node A's replica is a backup, so it refuses the request with
   `TransientNotAccepted` (never admitted).
2. `send_raw_vsr_attempt` replays the refusal on the same connection every 50 ms
   until `TRANSIENT_FAILOVER_CHECK_INTERVAL` (2 s) expires.
3. `send_raw_retaining_header` then takes `routing_lock` and `continue`s
   ("a concurrent refused request may have moved the shared client"), so a
   second 2 s replay window runs on the same node.
4. Only then does it check the metadata leader, walk the roster
   (`RosterWalk`, `settle_on_endpoint`), disconnect, and reconnect and sign in
   on the next node. The send succeeds there.
5. The next send goes to partition 1, whose primary is node A. Steps 1-4 repeat
   in the other direction: 4 s of refusals on node B, then a redirect back to
   the metadata leader.

A producer that spreads its sends over the partitions with
`Partitioning::messages_key(..)` or explicit partition ids hits this on almost
every send. Throughput is capped by the 4 s stall, not by the server, and the
server sits nearly idle.

**Expected:** a send reaches its partition's primary without the session moving
on every send, the way polls already do. Once the primaries are known, a
producer alternating between partitions should pay no refusal window and no
reconnect.

**Actual:** every send to a partition whose primary is not the connected node
waits out two transient windows (about 4 s), then moves the session. With two or
more primaries in play this happens on nearly every send.

## Affected area / component

Rust SDK, Clustering / replication

## Deployment

Compiled from source

## Versions

- Rust SDK `iggy` 0.11.0 (released) against a 3-node cluster built from
  `f6dfbdbb3` with unrelated patches: observed (numbers below).
- `master` @ `43fb44364`: failing integration test (PR linked below), 3 of 3
  runs.
- Tag `iggy-0.11.0` (`71f29618b`): the same test fails the same way.

The Go SDK (`foreign/go`) looks the same from reading the code, but I didn't
run it. `SendMessages` resolves the partition client side and then goes through
`c.do`. On `ErrTransientNotAccepted` that replays for `failoverCheckInterval`
(2 s), redirects to the leader or walks the roster with
`settleOnNextEndpoint`, and reconnects. There is no primary routing for sends.

## Hardware / environment

- Observed: 3-node cluster on Kubernetes, 2 CPU / 8 GiB per node. 12 producers,
  batches of 100 messages, 45k msg/s offered.
- Reproduced: the integration harness (3 nodes on localhost) in a Linux x86_64
  container (4 CPUs), pinned toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`.

## Reproduction

A failing test is on branch `test/sdk-send-partition-primary-routing` (PR
linked below). It is `#[ignore]`d with this issue's number, so run it with
`--ignored`:

```bash
cargo build --bin iggy-server
cargo test -p integration --test mod -- --ignored --exact \
  cluster::partition_primary_routing::given_partitions_on_different_primaries_when_sending_round_robin_should_keep_the_session
```

It uses the existing `seed_split_primaries` fixture in
`core/integration/tests/cluster/partition_primary_routing.rs`. Partition 0 stays
on its primary while a metadata-only election moves the metadata leader. It then
adds partition 1 with `create_partitions`. A partition created after the
election is seeded from the metadata view, so its primary is the metadata leader.
The test checks this precondition with `GET_POLL_ROUTING`: the two partitions
report primaries on different nodes. It sends one warm-up message to each
partition. Then it sends 4 messages alternating between partitions 0 and 1, and
asserts that no send moves the session to another node.

## Logs

The test's failure on master (partition, node before, node after, send time):

```text
assertion `left == right` failed: a producer alternating between partition 0 (primary node 0) and partition 1 (primary node 2) must keep its session; 4 of 4 sends moved it to another node (partition, from node, to node, send time):
[(0, 2, 0, 4.020694671s), (1, 0, 2, 4.018801233s), (0, 2, 0, 4.019829788s), (1, 0, 2, 4.018055753s)]
```

The client log during that run, one send per pair of lines (node 2 at `:20016`
is the metadata leader and partition 1's primary, node 0 at `:20000` is
partition 0's primary):

```text
20:54:02.365 iggy::tcp::tcp_client: The request keeps being refused on 127.0.0.1:20016 while the roster names it the metadata leader; trying the next cluster node at 127.0.0.1:20000.
20:54:06.390 iggy::tcp::tcp_client: Current node is not leader, redirecting to leader at: 127.0.0.1:20016
20:54:10.408 iggy::tcp::tcp_client: The request keeps being refused on 127.0.0.1:20016 while the roster names it the metadata leader; trying the next cluster node at 127.0.0.1:20000.
20:54:14.428 iggy::tcp::tcp_client: Current node is not leader, redirecting to leader at: 127.0.0.1:20016
```

Tag `iggy-0.11.0` gives the same pattern: `[(0, 2, 0, 4.068s), (1, 0, 2, 4.071s), (0, 2, 0, 4.081s), (1, 0, 2, 4.078s)]`.

Observed on the real cluster (SDK 0.11.0, 12 producers, batches of 100,
45k msg/s offered). The server logs `rejecting client request on non-primary
partition replica` for the refused sends:

| topic | primaries | achieved | send p50 | send p99 | server CPU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 partitions, fresh cluster | all on one node | 46k msg/s | - | 21 ms | - |
| 6 partitions, after three single-node restarts | spread over nodes | 11,984 msg/s | 2.6 ms | 4,054 ms | 0.1-0.2 cores |
| 1 partition, same load | one primary | 45,830 msg/s | - | 10 ms | - |

The 4,054 ms p99 matches the two 2 s windows per misrouted send.

## Code references (`master` @ `43fb44364`)

- `core/sdk/src/tcp/tcp_client.rs:83`: `TRANSIENT_FAILOVER_CHECK_INTERVAL = 2s`.
- `core/sdk/src/tcp/tcp_client.rs:1699-1704` (`send_raw_vsr_attempt`): replays
  `TransientNotAccepted` on the same connection until the transient deadline.
- `core/sdk/src/tcp/tcp_client.rs:1436-1445` (`send_raw_retaining_header`): the
  first refusal only takes `routing_lock` and `continue`s, so a second full
  window runs on the same node before any routing decision. This is where the
  4 s instead of 2 s comes from.
- `core/sdk/src/tcp/tcp_client.rs:1450-1525`: the leader check, then
  `RosterWalk` and `settle_on_endpoint` (`:1032`) move the session itself.
- `core/sdk/src/poll_routing.rs`: polls and offset writes get the partition
  primary (`GET_POLL_ROUTING`) and use a per-node data connection. Sends have no
  such path.

## Impact

- A producer writing several partitions loses most of its throughput after
  ordinary failovers (here 45k -> 12k msg/s), with 4 s tail latency and an idle
  server.
- Partition primaries stay where the failovers left them, so the stalls
  continue for as long as the primaries stay split.
- Every bounce is a disconnect, reconnect and sign-in, which adds session churn
  on the server.

## Suggested fix

Route sends like polls: resolve the target partition's primary and send over a
data connection to that node, keeping the session where it is. Cache the route
and refresh it on `TransientNotAccepted`. The existing `PollRouter` connection
pool, session binding and generation fencing look reusable. A send would need
the dedup identity of the connection it is sent on, as replicated offset writes
already have. A smaller step is to skip the second transient window. A refusal
proves the request was never admitted, so after taking `routing_lock` the
request could go straight to the routing decision instead of replaying for
another 2 s. That halves the stall but does not stop the bouncing. The Go SDK
would need the same change.

## Contribution

- [ ] I'm willing to submit a pull request to fix this bug
      (the failing test is ready as a PR; the fix is open for discussion)

Pyrefly v1.3.2

Release date: September 28, 2026

Pyrefly v1.3.2 is a patch release that fixes regressions in how Pyrefly infers the type of a variable after it is assigned a value of type Any.

Pyrefly v1.3.2

Release date: September 28, 2026

Pyrefly v1.3.2 is a patch release that fixes regressions in how Pyrefly infers the type of a variable after it is assigned a value of type Any.

Release notes

Sourced from ch.qos.logback:logback-classic's releases.

Logback 1.6.4

2026-09-24 Release of logback version 1.6.4

• Variable substitution is again applied to the scan attribute of the <configuration> element. The scanning refactoring in version 1.5.27 had dropped substitution, so values such as ${logback.scan.enabled:-true} were no longer resolved. As before version 1.5.27, an unrecognized non-empty value turns scanning on. The same substitution now applies to the scan attribute of <propertiesConfigurator>. This regression was reported in issues/1065 by vaibhavjain2.

• OutputStreamAppender and FileAppender now handle stateful encoders. The Encoder interface has a new default method called isStateful(), which returns false. An encoder that keeps state between calls to encode() can return true. For such encoders, the appender holds its write lock while encoding and while writing, so the output of concurrent appends cannot interleave. Stateless encoders still encode outside the lock, so their performance does not change. Existing encoders need no changes.

• Several race conditions in OutputStreamAppender and FileAppender were fixed. The appender is now marked started and the encoder header is written while the same lock is held, so a concurrent append can no longer write an event before the header. After acquiring the lock, the appender checks again whether it has been stopped, so no event is written after the footer. In prudent mode, FileAppender now encodes and writes each event while holding the lock.

• Fixed a data race on the logger count in LoggerContext. Loggers are created under the lock of their parent logger, so loggers with different parents could be created at the same time and increments of the shared counter could be lost. As a result, LoggerContext.size() could return a value lower than the actual number of loggers. The counter is now an AtomicInteger. This issue was reported in issues/1038 by hcantunc. The fix was contributed in PR #1055 by seonwoo_jung.

items.body:
## Which issue does this PR address?

N/A

## Rationale

`upstream/master` still declares Python 3.10 as supported. This change raises the Python SDK minimum to 3.11 and aligns package metadata, development environments, examples, and wheel builds with that decision. It currently removes 3.10 support directly, without a prior deprecation notice.

## What changed?

- Raise the minimum supported Python version from 3.10 to 3.11 across the SDK, BDD tests, examples, interpreter pins, CI configuration, and documentation.
- Regenerate the lock files for the supported range, removing Python 3.10-only dependencies and wheel records. Update the example enum to use `StrEnum`.
- Keep the generated `Durability` stub consistent with the runtime enum. A targeted `UP042` suppression prevents Ruff from suggesting a change with different `str()` behavior.
- Derive Linux and macOS wheel interpreters from the SDK’s Python classifiers, align the Windows matrix, and verify the Python compatibility metadata in release artifacts.

## Points for discussion

1. **`UP042` suppression:** Should the targeted `noqa` remain? Removing only the marker fails Ruff; changing the stub to `StrEnum` would describe different `str(Durability.REPLICATED)` behavior. Changing the runtime enum as well would change observable SDK behavior and needs an explicit compatibility decision.
2. **Python SDK version:** The SDK remains at `0.9.1.dev1`. Which version should first enforce Python 3.11: the `0.9.1` line, a new minor line such as `0.10.0`, or another planned release? Once decided, `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, and release tags should agree.
3. **Announcement timing:** Which Iggy release should first announce Python 3.10 deprecation, and which SDK release should actually stop supporting it? Should the Iggy website prominently call out the new Python 3.11 minimum in the Python SDK documentation and release notes?

## Local Execution

- Passed: Rust extension unit tests (20); Python 3.11 unit tests (220), non-TLS integration tests (613), Docker TLS tests (6), Docker BDD scenarios (4), and the Python examples including TLS.
- Passed: Python 3.12.15 and 3.13.16 unit tests (220 each) in Docker; interpreter synchronization and all three `uv.lock` checks.

labels.name: gateways
labels.description: proxy gateways for other protocols like kafka

items.body:
Part of #3560. Split out of #3543, which shipped `LeaveGroup` (13) in #4270.

## Summary

Implement KIP-345 static membership for Kafka consumer groups in the gateway.

Today `group.instance.id` (JoinGroup v5+) is stored, echoed back to the leader and seeds the generated member id, but nothing else is honoured (see "Static membership is accepted, not honoured" in `gateways/kafka/docs/CONSUMER_GROUPS.md`). A returning static member gets a new member id and its join triggers a rebalance, while its previous incarnation keeps its partitions until its session expires and triggers a second rebalance. Kafka replaces the old identity with no rebalance at all.

## Scope

- [ ] A JoinGroup with a known `group_instance_id` replaces the previous holder's member id without a rebalance (Kafka's `updateStaticMemberAndRebalance` path, including the leader case)
- [ ] One instance id maps to at most one member at a time
- [ ] `FENCED_INSTANCE_ID` (82) from `JoinGroup`, `SyncGroup` and `Heartbeat` when the member id does not hold the instance id it names, not only from `LeaveGroup`
- [ ] Session expiry of a static member still evicts it and rebalances
- [ ] `LeaveGroup` by instance id keeps Kafka's semantics once there is a single holder
- [ ] Update `CONSUMER_GROUPS.md` and the parity table

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Test: a static member restarts within `session.timeout.ms` and gets its partitions back with no generation bump
- [ ] Test: a stale incarnation of a replaced static member is fenced with 82 on Heartbeat and SyncGroup
- [ ] E2E with the Java client using `group.instance.id` (can ride on #3544)

items.title: Refuse a new consumer kind until every replica can decode it

labels.name: server
labels.description: iggy-server related change

labels.name: rust
labels.description: Pull requests that update Rust code

items.body:
### Description

#4392 adds the consumer kind `ExternalGroup` (wire value 3). During a rolling upgrade from `server-0.9.0`, a new primary admits kind 3 (`fence_group_offset` in `core/server/src/namespace.rs`). A `server-0.9.0` backup fails `WireConsumer::decode` on it before it appends the prepare. That backup never sends `PrepareOk`, and journal repair fails on the op in the same way. With 2 of 3 replicas still on `server-0.9.0`, the partition stops committing. `core/server/README.md` tells operators to upgrade every server before any external group store, but nothing enforces it. The Kafka gateway stores kind 3 on every consumer offset commit, so one commit during an upgrade can stop a partition. Raised in the review of #4392.

### Affected area / component

Iggy server

### Proposed solution

Make each replica send its release, and let the primary refuse kind 3 until every replica runs a release that decodes it. The consensus headers have a `release` field, but nothing fills it yet.

### Alternatives considered

Keep the rule in `core/server/README.md` as the only guard. Or add a cluster setting that allows kind 3 stores, and let the operator turn it on after the upgrade.

items.title: feat(gateways): answer OffsetCommit and OffsetFetch

labels.name: S-waiting-on-review
labels.description: PR is waiting on a reviewer

items.body:
Closes #3542

With `IGGY_KAFKA_BRIDGE_ENABLED=true`, OffsetCommit (8) and OffsetFetch (9) now keep group offsets in Iggy, using the `ExternalGroup` kind from #4392. A group resumes from its last commit, also after a gateway restart, and `kafka-console-consumer.sh --group` commits and resumes.

### How offsets are stored

- key: the partition, plus Iggy consumer group `kafka.cg.<group>` on the mapped topic. The gateway creates that group on the first commit and never joins it
- value: the Kafka offset as sent, no range check. 0 on an empty partition and one past the last message both work
- a negative offset deletes the key. Metadata and leader epoch are dropped, OffsetFetch returns `""` and -1
- nothing deletes these groups on its own. `OFFSET_STORAGE.md` has the `iggy consumer-group delete` command for cleanup

### Commit and fetch

- OffsetCommit v2-v9 checks the committer the way Kafka's `validateOffsetCommit` does. After a gateway restart a member gets `UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID` and rejoins. Admin tools commit with a negative generation, which works on an empty group
- OffsetFetch v1-v9, batched groups from v8. A null topic list (`Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets`) reads every topic that holds the group
- no key, no group or no topic reads as -1 with no error. Any other failed read fails the whole group instead, because a consumer that gets -1 resets its position
- retriable failures go back as 14, `RequestTooOld` too. Java fails offset calls on 6, and OffsetFetch on 7. A replay that already landed (`RequestAlreadyApplied`) counts as done
- anything sent as -1 is logged at `error!` with the group and the cause

### Iggy calls

- offset calls run on 4 slots, and each slot has one Iggy client for commits and one for reads. Reads never wait behind a commit, and nothing waits behind Produce. The topic listing for a null topic list runs on a slot too
- a request keeps at most one call queued per slot, so one big request (a null topic list over many topics, say) can't hold up the others. Inside that, its partitions, the groups of a v8 fetch and the topics of a null topic list run at once
- each partition sticks to one slot, and a topic's partitions take the slots in turn. A commit holds its slot until it ends, 45s at most. Commits on a slot share one client that sends one call at a time, which keeps them in order even when a caller gives up. A read frees its slot at the deadline
- a request gives up after half the min session timeout (3s by default). Heartbeats on the same connection wait behind it, so a request also gives up after half of what's left of the session of the member that heartbeats there. Partitions cut off by that answer 14 without a call

### Server change

`get_consumer_offset` answered a read that timed out on the owning shard, or found the partition not loaded there, with an empty body. Over HTTP the not-loaded case was a 404. The SDK reads both as "no offset", and a consumer would reset. Both now answer `TransientNotAccepted` (503 over HTTP), which the Rust SDK retries. This is in `core/server/src/dispatch/partition.rs` and `core/server/src/http/handlers.rs` and applies to every client.

### Known limits

- every Iggy server needs a build with kind 3 (#4392) before the first commit. Nothing enforces that yet, and in a partly upgraded cluster one commit can stop a partition from committing
- in a cluster an offset read can land on a node that lags. Right after a group's first commit that node answers -1, and a consumer on `auto.offset.reset=latest` skips records. Reads from the primary are #4409
- with more than one gateway, a commit with no generation on a gateway without the group's members overwrites the live offsets, and a commit a gateway gave up on can land after a newer one from another gateway. Both are in `OFFSET_STORAGE.md`
- delivery stays at-least-once

### Description

`handle_get_consumer_offset` answers from the local replica of the partition (see the TODO above it in `core/server/src/dispatch/partition.rs`). The SDK sends the read to the node it is connected to, and that node can be a backup that lags the partition's primary. Iggy server, Rust SDK

Route the read to the partition primary, the way `GET_CONSUMER_OFFSET_ROUTING_CODE` routes offset writes. Gate it on the server with `is_caught_up_primary`, as the auto-commit path does.

### Alternatives considered

Define a follower-read contract, and let a caller that needs read-your-commits route the read itself.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: server
labels.description: iggy-server related change

labels.name: rust
labels.description: Pull requests that update Rust code

items.body:
### Bug description

The REST API cannot name a consumer kind. `Consumer.kind` is `#[serde(skip)]`, and the server builds a plain consumer (`Consumer::new`) from an HTTP request. An HTTP client can pass `Consumer::group(..)` to `store_consumer_offset`, `get_consumer_offset`, `delete_consumer_offset` or `poll_messages`. The call then acts on the plain consumer with the group's id, and no error tells the caller. Join and leave already return `FeatureUnavailable` over HTTP, so a group cannot work there.

Expected: the HTTP client refuses every kind except `ConsumerKind::Consumer` with `FeatureUnavailable`, as #4392 does for `ConsumerKind::ExternalGroup` (`refuse_external_group` in `core/sdk/src/http/consumer_offsets.rs`). This changes behavior for an HTTP caller that passes a group today. Raised in the review of #4392.

### Affected area / component

Rust SDK, Iggy server

### Reproduction

1. Build an `IggyClient` with the HTTP transport.
2. Send 10 messages to partition 0 of a topic.
3. Store offset 5 with `Consumer::group(Identifier::numeric(1)?)` on partition 0.
4. Read the offset with `Consumer::new(Identifier::numeric(1)?)`. It returns 5.

labels.name: S-waiting-on-review
labels.description: PR is waiting on a reviewer

items.body:
The cluster tests inject scripted faults at chosen points, for
example one SIGKILL of a backup or of the primary. No test kept
producers, consumer groups and segment expiry running while nodes
died one after another.

The new test SIGKILLs one random node of five every interval and
restarts it with its data. Message ids carry the producer and the
sequence, so the test can account for every acknowledged message
without trusting payloads. At the end, it compares the nodes over
HTTP and, after a clean stop, their segment files byte for byte.
A second topic without expiry keeps the full history for these
compares, because expiry leaves only active segments.

The module doc lists the server gaps that a run can hit or that
limit its checks.

It is opt-in (#[ignore]) because it runs for minutes. A nextest
override runs it alone, so other tests do not skew the kill
timing, and allows up to one hour for long runs. Its knobs use
the IGGY_TEST_ prefix of the other harness variables. The harness
forwards every IGGY_* variable to the servers, and a debug server
refuses to boot on an unknown one, so the boot check now accepts
that prefix instead of three listed names.

## Which issue does this PR address?

Closes  #3548
Relates #3560 

## Rationale

`kafka-consumer-groups.sh` and other admin clients learn classic group membership by sending DescribeGroups and ListGroups. This gateway already coordinates those groups in memory for join, heartbeat, sync, and leave, and nothing on the wire would report that state, so those tools could not inspect a group on this coordinator.

## What changed?

DescribeGroups versions 0-6 and ListGroups versions 0-5 now read that same in-memory coordinator. A live group is `PreparingRebalance`, `CompletingRebalance`, or `Stable`. A named group that is not in the map is `Dead`. Version 6 also returns `GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND` (69) and `Group {id} not found.`. Older describe versions return `Dead` with error 0, because a v6 client treats error 0 as a group that exists.

Each member includes its id, its instance id, the subscription metadata of the selected protocol, and its assignment bytes. `client_id` and `client_host` stay empty, because the coordinator does not retain the request header's client id or the connection's peer address. `include_authorized_operations` stays at the omitted sentinel. There is no group ACL bitfield. ListGroups sets `group_type` to `classic`. From v4 a state filter, and from v5 a type filter, keep a group only when the filter is empty or one entry matches, case-insensitively after trim. A filter value this coordinator does not use matches nothing, and the response error stays 0.

ListGroups does not expire sessions. Expiry runs on a request that names a group, and a list names none, so listing must not open rebalances as a side effect of reading. DescribeGroups ticks each named group once, after the requested ids are deduped, so a repeated id is one group and one tick. The describe frame is priced from lengths already stored, before any member snapshot is copied. If that body would exceed `max_frame_size`, the connection closes. An oversized ListGroups body closes the same way. The list is priced before it is encoded, because the request shape guard never sees the groups that will be written back.

Join rejects a `protocol_type`, a client-supplied `member_id`, or a `group_instance_id` longer than `i16::MAX`. DescribeGroups v0-v4 and ListGroups v0-v2 encode those fields as legacy strings, and a longer value cannot be written back. When the member id is generated, the instance id is the prefix and 37 bytes are reserved for `-{uuid}`, so the id itself still fits that cap. A failed DescribeGroups decode closes the connection: the response has no top-level error field, and an empty group list would look like success. A failed ListGroups decode returns `INVALID_REQUEST` (42). Groups stay in process memory only. A restart drops membership. Committed offsets stay in Iggy.

items.body:
### Description

Add a Google BigQuery sink connector (`core/connectors/sinks/bigquery_sink`) that writes messages from Iggy topics into BigQuery tables using the **BigQuery Storage Write API**.

## Scope

- Write via the Storage Write API `_default` stream using Arrow-encoded rows. Do not use the legacy `insertAll` API.
- Authentication:
  - Service account key from a file or inline secret.
  - Google Application Default Credentials (ADC).
- Configuration:
  - `project_id`
  - `dataset`
  - `table`
  - retries/backoff
  - timeout
  - maximum request size
- Support two ingestion modes:
  - **`mapped`**: JSON payload fields map to BigQuery table columns. Fetch and validate the target table schema during `open()`.
  - **`raw`**: Store the original payload in a single column alongside optional Iggy metadata.
- Optional Iggy metadata columns:
  - `iggy_stream`
  - `iggy_topic`
  - `iggy_partition_id`
  - `iggy_offset`
  - `iggy_timestamp`
  - `iggy_id`
  - `iggy_headers`
- Payload support:
  - JSON
  - Text
  - Raw payloads in `raw` mode
  - JSON representations of Protobuf payloads where applicable
- In `mapped` mode, Text payloads are parsed as JSON. Rows that are not valid JSON objects are rejected.
- Columns missing from a JSON payload use BigQuery's `DEFAULT_VALUE` missing-value interpretation by default, with `NULL_VALUE` configurable where appropriate.
- Split large batches below the Storage Write API `AppendRows` request limit, using a conservative threshold such as ~8 MB.
- No buffering across `consume()` calls.
- Unsupported BigQuery column types such as `INTERVAL` and `RANGE` should fail validation during `open()`.

## Error handling

Retry transient/retryable gRPC failures with bounded jittered backoff, including:

- `UNAVAILABLE`
- `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`
- `INTERNAL`
- `ABORTED`
- `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`

Treat errors such as the following as permanent:

- `INVALID_ARGUMENT`
- `PERMISSION_DENIED`
- `UNAUTHENTICATED`

For row-level errors, identify the offending rows, drop them, and re-append the remaining valid rows once. Every dropped row must be logged with its stream, topic, partition, and offset and counted in a connector metric.

There is no dead-letter queue in v1.

## Delivery guarantees

The connector runtime commits consumer group offsets when messages are polled, before `consume()` runs. A batch for which `consume()` returns an error is logged and not redelivered.

Consequences:

- The sink retries retryable BigQuery failures internally with bounded backoff.
- A batch that still fails after the final retry, or encounters a permanent error, is lost.
- A process crash between the consumer group offset commit and a successful BigQuery append also loses that batch.
- With the `_default` stream, an ambiguous append result followed by a retry can produce duplicates. The `iggy_stream`, `iggy_topic`, `iggy_partition_id`, and `iggy_offset` metadata can be used for downstream deduplication.

Crash-safe delivery guarantees, whether at-least-once or exactly-once, require a runtime change so consumer group offsets are committed only after the sink successfully persists the batch. This should be tracked separately.

Future work may use committed write streams with explicit append offsets for stronger in-process delivery guarantees.

## Implementation

- Use `gcloud-bigquery` (Apache-2.0) for the Storage Write API, table metadata, and authentication. It aligns with workspace dependencies including `arrow`, `reqwest`, and `prost`.
- `tonic` (with the `server` feature) is added as a dev-dependency of the integration test crate for the fake BigQueryWrite service. The sink itself reaches gRPC through `gcloud-bigquery`; `tonic` is already present transitively in `Cargo.lock`.
- Follow existing sink connector conventions, including the `clickhouse_sink` layout, SDK retry helpers, secrets kept out of logs, and atomic counters.

## Testing

### Unit tests

Cover:

- Configuration and validation
- Schema mapping
- Arrow encoding
- Request-size splitting
- Error classification
- Retry behavior
- Row-level error handling
- Credential source selection:
  - key file
  - inline key
  - ADC fallback
  - missing/invalid key file

### Integration tests

Use an in-process fake BigQuery service consisting of a `tonic` BigQueryWrite service and HTTP `tables.get` stub.

Cover:

- Successful writes
- Batch splitting
- Row-level errors
- Retryable failures
- Permanent failures
- `PERMISSION_DENIED` and `UNAUTHENTICATED` responses treated as permanent errors
- Schema validation failures during `open()`

A real BigQuery dependency should not be required for CI. Document manual verification against Google BigQuery in the connector README.

## Documentation

Add:

- Connector README
- Configuration reference
- Required Google Cloud IAM permissions
- Authentication examples
- BigQuery/Iggy type mapping
- Delivery guarantees and failure semantics
- Manual testing instructions
- Sample TOML under `runtime/example_config/connectors/`
- BigQuery entry in the sinks README

## Non-goals for v1

- Automatic table creation
- Automatic schema evolution
- Per-topic table routing
- CDC upserts/deletes using `_CHANGE_TYPE`
- Crash-safe delivery guarantees (requires a connector runtime change)
- Dead-letter queue for rejected rows

items.title: feat(server): store offsets of groups managed outside Iggy
items.body:
## Which issue does this PR address?

  Relates to #3542

  ## Rationale

  The Kafka gateway needs to keep a committed offset for every Kafka group, topic and partition. The accepted design in `gateways/kafka/docs/OFFSET_STORAGE.md` stores it as an Iggy consumer group offset under `kafka.cg.<group>`. That kind does not fit
  the gateway:

  - The server lets only a member that owns the partition write a group offset, and the gateway never joins the group.
  - The server refuses an offset past the last message. Kafka commits the next offset to read, which is one past the last message, and it can commit 0 on an empty partition.
  - A group offset holds back retention. A Kafka committed offset never does.
  - An Iggy consumer that polls that key with `Next` skips one record per partition, and only a naming rule stops it.

  The gateway handlers and the update to that design doc come in a separate PR.

  ## What changed?

Group offsets had to come from a member of an Iggy consumer group, inside the partition's range, and they held back retention. A new consumer kind, `ExternalGroup` (wire value 3, `Consumer::external_group` in the Rust SDK), now stores offsets for a group that lives outside Iggy. The key is the numeric id of an existing Iggy consumer group, so the gateway still creates that group but never joins it. These offsets have their own key space, so they never share a key with the group's own offsets.

  For this kind the server:

  - accepts a store or a delete for any existing group, with no membership check
  - stores the value as sent, with no range check and no clamp at boot
  - refuses a poll with `FeatureUnavailable`
  - leaves it out of the retention barrier
  - deletes the offsets of a deleted group, through the same replicated delete as group offsets

  The server replicates these offsets, recovers them at boot from `offsets/external_groups/`, carries them in partition state transfer, and clears them on a purge. Boot creates that directory for a partition that an older build made. The HTTP client
  returns `FeatureUnavailable` for this kind, because the REST API cannot name a consumer kind. The CLI accepts `--kind external-group`.

  Some changes elsewhere follow from the new kind:

  - A caught-up primary now serves a state transfer of an empty partition with committed ops. A client can store and then delete an offset on a partition that never took a message. Before, a backup behind the repair floor had no way past those ops.
  - A purge whose offset directory sync fails leaves its generation unrecorded, so the reconciler runs it again. Boot never clamps an external offset, so without this a crash can bring back a deleted one.
  - A state transfer install syncs `offsets/` after the kind directories. The commit walk syncs it once per walk, not once per kind.

Relates to #4287

An explicit `disconnect()` must hold until the next `connect()`, as agreed on #4287: the test in `disconnect_relogin.rs` is the correct contract, not the `IggyClient` docs. Problems 2 and 3 of #4287 break this rule for a client with auto-login credentials. This PR fixes these two problems.

## What changed?

After `disconnect()`, a client with auto-login credentials came back on its own. The heartbeat kept running and its ping reconnected the client and signed in again, and a direct `ping()` or `get_stats()` did the same. Only an authenticated request such as `get_me()` failed, because `fail_if_not_authenticated` rejects it before the transport.

Now the `Client` trait impl of `disconnect()` sets a caller-intent flag on TCP, QUIC and WebSocket, and the trait impl of `connect()` clears it. While the flag is set, `send_raw_with_response` fails with `NotConnected` at once: no packets on the wire, no wait, no reconnect. The flag lives only in the trait impl, because leader redirection and the reconnect path call the inherent `disconnect()`. items.title: feat(consensus): persist retry receipts and shared sessions

labels.name: breaking:storage
labels.description: On-disk data format change - skips backwards compat CI

items.body:
Lost replies and retry-cache eviction could allow duplicate mutations after promotion or restart. This PR persists retry protection for shared sessions and publishes receipt checkpoints before reclaiming the corresponding WAL. Retained receipts replay the original result for the same session, group, request ID and operation, subject to current authorization. A partition session retains the highest applied request ID's receipt; committing an out-of-order lower request does not replace it. Already-applied requests without a retained outcome return `RequestTooOld`.

Shared sessions use client-owned binding proof, authenticated lease renewal and ordered retirement. Partition retirement barriers batch up to 128 ended sessions. Finalization still requires reports covering every allocated partition from a common replica quorum. Reports track a separate partition-incarnation revision; purge and segment deletion do not reset retirement progress. `clients_table_max` and `dedup_clients_max` become committed per-group limits, preserved across recovery and transfer. Live protection is not evicted to admit new clients.

Durable initialization records outside partition directories distinguish partitions that never initialized from initialized partitions whose history was lost. Missing history keeps initialized partitions fenced pending recovery. A permanently failed partition counts toward retirement only after publishing a durable incarnation fence. Replacing its files or restarting does not clear that fence; failure to persist it keeps the session retained.

Metadata snapshot installation and log-tail replay preserve revoked-session history and newer retry protection. HTTP JWT requests and write-session attachment recheck that the owner exists and is active against locally applied metadata.

Compatibility and limits:

- This changes wire and storage formats. Unsupported existing data directories are refused before modification. No migration or rolling-upgrade adapter is supplied; servers and compatible clients deploy together. New empty roots initialize automatically, but complete metadata-directory loss is outside automatic recovery guarantees. Preserve the external initialization and retirement records with backups.
- Development protocol bounds are `0.11.1..=0.11.1`, including patch. Final stable-release bounds remain to be chosen. Released protocol 0.11.0 servers accept every 0.11.x patch, so an incompatible release needs a new minor version for those servers to reject it. Intermediate builds may share a number while requiring different layouts.
- Replica admission compares protocol, release and storage-format identity. Stripping or repackaging an otherwise compatible executable does not change that identity.
- Crash-safe send retries require `Persisted`; explicit offset retries require `Persisted` and `Quorum`. `Replicated` remains the default and uses buffered partition WAL writes without a per-send persistence barrier. HTTP `ack=none` confirms dispatch only; same-session/partition writes wait for the prior reply or bounded deadline. Purge preserves retained send receipts without restoring purged messages.
- The binding proof is an independent session credential. Password changes and PAT revocation or expiry do not end an established session. Logout, lease expiry and user deactivation/deletion end session access. Current permissions govern requests, including receipt replays.
- Rust `ConsensusSession::bind` and `next_request_id` now return `Result`. External `VsrSessionControl` implementations must provide `session_identity` and `session_bind_secret`. Explicit disconnect clears remembered login and local identity; configured AutoLogin can authenticate a later connection.
- Rust producers create fresh binary retry attempts only after `TransientNotAccepted` or proven presubmission `NotConnected`/`CannotEstablishConnection`. HTTP failures use separate transport retry settings. Uncertain and terminal failures return the unconfirmed batch; an application resend can duplicate an earlier uncertain mutation. Receipt access after permission revocation and general replica-routing/cancellation APIs remain follow-up work.

Rust, Go, Java, C#, Node and Rust-backed bindings use the coordinated login/binding contract. Established Go/Java/C# sessions resume coordinator connections with `BindSession`, retaining identity and sequence; terminal `Unauthenticated` or `StaleClient` bind refusals permit fresh registration. Swift golden fixtures and error mirrors are updated from Rust.

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good for newcomers

labels.name: connectors
labels.description: Connectors runtime

items.body:
### Description

`field_mappings` silently loses or misroutes data in three pre-existing
cases. None of the 9 config types that carry `field_mappings` validate it.
All three are edge cases. A bad config (two mappings onto one target, or
two proto fields sharing a JSON name) is the likelier trigger. Payloads
that already contain the target key or duplicate keys are more rare.

1. **Rename collision drops a value.** Two keys rename onto one target,
   or a rename lands on a key already in the payload. One value is
   dropped. Which one survives is unspecified once simd_json switches to
   its hash-backed map (over 32 keys).
2. **Duplicate keys in incoming JSON.** simd_json keeps every duplicate
   when parsing (`{"a":1,"a":2}` parses with `len() == 2`), so a naive
   runtime collision check (`insert(..).is_some()`) fails on payloads
   whose mapped keys never collide. Real producers rarely emit
   duplicate keys.
3. **Proto encoder reverse lookup is ambiguous.** `ProtoStreamEncoder`
   maps JSON name to proto name with `.find()` over a `HashMap`. If two
   mappings share a JSON name, the proto field chosen depends on
   per-process hash order, so a restart can change the wire field.

### Affected area / component

Connectors

### Proposed solution

Decide the policy first, then apply it across all 9 config types:

- Config load: reject duplicate JSON names in `ProtoEncoderConfig` (3).
  For many-to-one targets (1), decide whether aliasing two source names
  onto one key is legitimate, since a config check alone cannot tell
  aliasing from a real collision.
- Runtime: decide how duplicate-keyed JSON (2) is handled before adding
  any per-message collision check.

### Alternatives considered

- Sort candidates in the proto encoder for a deterministic winner.
- Warn on collision at runtime. This runs per message, so it needs
  once, rate-limited or metric-based reporting rather than a plain `warn!`.
- Enable simd_json's `value-no-dup-keys` to reject duplicates at parse time.

### Bug description

`BytesSerializer.toBytes(Map<HeaderKey, HeaderValue>)` builds an error message for every header it encodes, even when the header is valid.

The length checks at lines 123 and 129 pass a ready-made string:

```java
checkFieldLength(key.value().length, "key '" + key + "'");
checkFieldLength(value.value().length, "value for key '" + key + "'");
```

Each call runs `HeaderKey.toString()`, which decodes the key bytes into a new `String`, and then concatenates. That happens twice per header on every message sent. The string is only used when the check fails.

Suggested fix: only build the message when the check fails, for example:

```java
if (key.value().length < 1 || key.value().length > MAX_HEADER_FIELD_LENGTH) {
    checkFieldLength(key.value().length, "key '" + key + "'");
}
```

and the same for the value. The error text stays the same.

Measured with SDK 0.9.0 on a local laptop, encoding batches of 1,000 messages with 100-byte payloads and one user header each: about 116 to 136 ns per message before the change, 91 to 98 ns after, roughly a quarter less.

items.title: fix(sdk): keep a shut down client shut down
items.body:
## Which issue does this PR address?

Relates to #4287

## Rationale

`shutdown()` must be final, as agreed on #4287: a client that is shut down must not connect again, whatever the caller does next. Problems 1 and 4 of #4287 break this rule. This PR fixes these two problems. Problems 2 and 3, about `disconnect()`, come in a separate PR.

## What changed?

A client that was shut down could come back. `WebSocketClient` dialed again on `connect()`, because its `connect_inner` had no `Shutdown` arm. On every transport, a `disconnect()` after `shutdown()` wrote `Disconnected` over `Shutdown`, so `connect()` worked again.

Now one guard in `set_state` keeps `Shutdown` final on TCP, QUIC and WebSocket, so no later write can revive the client. This guard also covers the `Disconnected` writes that other paths add, for example a timeout. `WebSocketClient::connect_inner` also returns `ClientShutdown` before any dial, as TCP and QUIC already do. The guard alone does not stop that dial.

The `Client` trait now documents this contract on `shutdown()`. The two lifecycle tests from #4344 for these cases lose their `#[ignore]`. On the Python side, the strict `xfail` of the WebSocket case and the known-issue note of `shutdown()` go away, because the bug is fixed.

## Local Execution

I used Zed in devcontainer mode. The build and the tests ran in the devcontainer, and `prek` ran on macOS.

- Passed: `cargo fmt --all` and `cargo clippy -p iggy_common -p iggy -p integration --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- Passed: `cargo test -p iggy --lib`, with 232 tests.
- Passed: the lifecycle tests. The 4 cases of problems 1 and 4 pass, and the 6 cases of problems 2 and 3 stay ignored:

  ```text
  $ cargo test -p integration -- sdk::client_lifecycle
  test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 6 ignored; 0 measured; 991 filtered out
  ```

- Passed: the `sdk::` integration suite (63 passed, 6 ignored), in two runs, and the `cluster::` suite (80 passed), because the guard changes state transitions that reconnects and failovers use.
- Passed: the Python lifecycle tests against a local server, with no `xfail` left:

  ```text
  $ uv run --no-sync pytest tests/test_connectivity.py -k Lifecycle
  16 passed, 35 deselected
  ```

- Passed: `cargo run --bin stub_gen`. The stub matches the edited docstring.
- Passed: pre-commit hooks with `SKIP=web-lint prek run --all-files`. I skipped `web-lint` because this PR does not change `web/`.

## AI Usage
